title: The Coverage Gap: Empirically Testing the 'Reward Hacking as Equilibrium' Axioms

original_idea.body:
# The Coverage Gap: Empirically Testing the 'Reward Hacking as Equilibrium' Axioms

**Problem:** A 2026 formal result proves that under finite evaluation, any optimized agent systematically under-invests effort in quality dimensions its evaluator does not cover, making reward hacking a structural equilibrium. The causal link 'uncovered quality dimension -> systematic under-investment' has a clean theoretical statement but little controlled empirical confirmation on real LLMs.

**Direction:** Design a multi-dimensional task (e.g., short essays scored on correctness, brevity, citation accuracy) where one dimension is deliberately left out of the visible rubric given to an open model. Use best-of-n against the partial rubric and measure whether quality on the hidden dimension monotonically degrades as optimization pressure rises — the precise prediction of the equilibrium theorem. Vary which dimension is hidden.

**Why it matters:** Turns an abstract impossibility-style theorem into a falsifiable experiment a beginner can run, and tests whether the predicted 'under-investment' actually appears. Confirming (or breaking) the theory's empirical reach is exactly the theory-empirics bridge the subfield context flags as missing.

**Relevant context:** 'Reward Hacking as Equilibrium under Finite Evaluation' (arXiv:2603.28063) — five minimal axioms predicting systematic under-investment in uncovered dimensions, unifying sycophancy/length-gaming/spec-gaming.
